research_brief:
**Definitions**

**Interview**
Polymer's talent acquisition article describes an interview as "an opportunity for you to see if the candidate is a good fit (and vice versa)," presenting a chance for both sides to ask questions and assess mutual fit. Source: Polymer, "What is talent acquisition? A complete guide," https://www.polymer.co/blog/talent-acquisition

**Structured interview**
A structured interview standardizes the questions and evaluation methods used: each candidate for the same role receives the same questions in the same order and is scored against the same criteria. Polymer describes the process as "using purposefully designed standardized questions and an interview scorecard (or interview rubric) to rate candidates based on their skills, experience, values, and cultural fit." Source: Polymer, "Behavioral Interview Scoring Matrix: A Template & Simple Guide," https://www.polymer.co/blog/behavioral-interview-scoring-matrix

**Unstructured interview**
An unstructured interview involves a relatively unplanned conversation with each candidate that differs across interviews, aiming to get a "feel for" the candidate rather than evaluating against a fixed set of criteria. Source: Glassdoor, "Terrific Interview Techniques for Interviewers and Interviewees," https://www.glassdoor.com/blog/guide/interview-techniques/

**Behavioral interview**
Behavioral interviews focus on actions candidates have taken in previous jobs; the interviewer assesses how people approached and resolved various work problems. The principle is that past performance can predict future behavior. Questions typically begin with "Tell me about a time when…" or "Give me an example of a time when…." Source: SHRM, "Interviewing Basics," https://www.shrm.org/mena/topics-tools/news/hr-magazine/interviewing-basics; Polymer, "What is talent acquisition? A complete guide," https://www.polymer.co/blog/talent-acquisition

**Situational interview**
Situational questions get at how candidates might react to a scenario or problem they could face in the new job — often hypothetical — using starters such as "What would you do if…" and "Tell me how you would handle…." They test a candidate's ability to think through problems, but may not illuminate prior work history. Source: SHRM, "Interviewing Basics," https://www.shrm.org/mena/topics-tools/news/hr-magazine/interviewing-basics; Polymer, "What is talent acquisition? A complete guide," https://www.polymer.co/blog/talent-acquisition

**Technical interview**
Common for engineering, data, and finance roles, a technical interview asks candidates to solve problems live, complete coding challenges, or walk through case analyses using tools and frameworks specific to the job. These are typically the longest individual interview format, running one to three hours. Source: Glassdoor, "How to prepare for a job interview," https://www.glassdoor.com/blog/guide/the-ultimate-job-interview-preparation-guide/

**Case interview**
Each applicant is given a hypothetical or existing business situation or problem to analyze, must draw on knowledge and creative abilities to propose a solution, and explains how they arrived at it. Common in consulting and strategy roles. Source: SHRM, "Interviewing Basics," https://www.shrm.org/mena/topics-tools/news/hr-magazine/interviewing-basics

**Panel interview**
A panel interview involves two or more interviewers — who may include HR representatives, hiring managers, and team leads — sitting together to question a single candidate. It gives multiple stakeholders ownership of the hiring decision and can eliminate the need for multiple separate rounds. Source: U.S. Department of Labor, "TEAMS Interview Skills Participant Guide 2026," https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/VETS/files/InterviewSkills_PG_Interactive_Feb2026.pdf

**Group interview**
In a group interview, several people from the hiring organization meet simultaneously with each candidate; panel members take turns asking questions, with some present only to observe. Source: SHRM, "Interviewing Basics," https://www.shrm.org/mena/topics-tools/news/hr-magazine/interviewing-basics

**Phone screening**
A phone screening is a brief, sometimes unscheduled call — as short as 10 minutes — in which an employer verifies basic qualifications, clarifies outstanding application questions, or confirms the candidate's continued interest, with the goal of creating a shortlist before a formal interview. Source: U.S. Department of Labor, "TEAMS Interview Skills Participant Guide 2026," https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/VETS/files/InterviewSkills_PG_Interactive_Feb2026.pdf

**Video interview**
A live video interview takes place online between employer and candidate. A one-way video interview uses a platform that presents pre-recorded questions, which the candidate answers while recording their responses. Source: U.S. Department of Labor, "TEAMS Interview Skills Participant Guide 2026," https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/VETS/files/InterviewSkills_PG_Interactive_Feb2026.pdf

**Final interview**
Not explicitly defined in the sources retrieved.

**Interview bias**
Polymer defines interview bias as "any preference or mental shortcut that shapes how an interviewer judges a candidate on factors unrelated to their ability to do the job." Common types include first impression bias, the halo and horns effect, affinity bias, confirmation bias, the contrast effect, recency and primacy bias, stereotype bias, and groupthink. Source: Polymer, "Interview Bias: The Types, Where It Creeps In, and How to Reduce It," https://www.polymer.co/blog/interview-bias

**Interview scoring / scorecard**
An interview scorecard lists predetermined criteria used to evaluate candidates; interviewers score each candidate against the criteria immediately after the interview. Polymer's behavioral interview scoring matrix uses this approach with a five-point rating scale. Source: Polymer, "Behavioral Interview Scoring Matrix: A Template & Simple Guide," https://www.polymer.co/blog/behavioral-interview-scoring-matrix

**Interview feedback**
Polymer defines interview feedback as "the final stage of the hiring process to close the interview process in a respectful manner," usually given to candidates who were not selected, explaining why and offering actionable guidance for improvement. Source: Polymer, "Interview Feedback Examples: What to Say and How to Deliver It," https://www.polymer.co/blog/interview-feedback-examples

---

**Unverified**

- Definition of a final interview as a distinct interview type: not found in any source retrieved.
- Polymer-specific definition of a phone screening, video interview, technical interview, case interview, panel interview, or group interview: Polymer does not publish standalone definitions for these types; definitions above are drawn from SHRM, the U.S. Department of Labor, and Glassdoor.

**Best practices**

**The Predictive Index — "Interview Best Practices for Hiring Managers"**
https://www.predictiveindex.com/blog/interview-best-practices-for-hiring-managers/

Build the scorecard before candidates arrive: "Scoring criteria defined after a strong candidate impresses you aren't criteria anymore." A useful scorecard includes competencies, a rating scale, space for specific examples and direct quotes, and an overall recommendation field. Brief the panel in advance — everyone should review the resume, job description, and screening notes before the interview, not during it. Follow the 80/20 rule: "Aim for the candidate to carry roughly 80% of the conversation. Resist the urge to fill silence, elaborate on the question, or jump in before the candidate has finished thinking." Root questions in real experience rather than hypotheticals; the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) gives candidates a structure and gives managers a consistent framework. When answers are vague or rehearsed, probe with follow-ups such as "What specifically did you do in that situation?" or "What would you handle differently now?"

**SocialTalent — "Interviewing 101: Best Practice Interview Techniques"**
https://www.socialtalent.com/interviewing/interviewing-best-practices

Define clear hiring criteria that separate must-haves from nice-to-haves before the process begins. Conduct structured screening calls to verify qualifications, motivation, and fit before progressing candidates. For panel debriefs, have the most junior interviewer speak first "so disagreement gets voiced before senior opinions set the tone." On bias: use diverse panels, standardized questions, and focus on culture-add rather than culture-fit. On feedback: "Offer specific, actionable feedback to candidates. Generic comments are of little value; detailed insights demonstrate respect and consideration."

**University of Wisconsin HR — "Best Practices for Employment Interviews"**
https://hr.wisc.edu/hr-professionals/recruitment/best-practices-for-employment-interviews/

For question pacing, allow approximately three minutes for single-scenario questions and closer to six minutes for multipart questions. Reserve at least ten minutes at the end for candidate questions. Consider sending interview questions at least 24 hours in advance to ease nerves and elicit more thoughtful answers. Assign specific questions to each panel member to ensure a structured and efficient process. Ensure all questions are consistent across candidates and avoid any that touch on arrest record, military status, pregnancy, age, religion, marital status, or other protected characteristics.

**Forbes — "Interviewing Etiquette 101: 15 Best Practices For Hiring Managers And Headhunters"**
https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbeshumanresourcescouncil/2023/01/04/interviewing-etiquette-101-15-best-practices-for-hiring-managers-and-headhunters/

Share an interview itinerary with candidates beforehand so they know what to expect. Finish the full interview with every candidate regardless of early impressions: "cutting an interview short, based on disinterest, invites reputational risk to a company." Disclose salary range up front. Never ask questions about protected characteristics — "managers should never leave a candidate wondering whether small talk about their place of worship or sexual orientation may have cost them the job."

---

**Unverified**

- Best practices specific to technical interviews and case interviews from an authoritative HR or academic source were not found in these results.
- Best practices for rejection communication from an independent editorial source (not an ATS vendor) were not surfaced in this search.

**Best practices: technical interviews**

**Source 1: HackerRank, "How to Conduct a Technical Interview: A Complete Guide for Hiring Teams," https://www.hackerrank.com/writing/how-to-conduct-a-technical-interview**

Before writing a single question, define what success looks like in the role for the first six months — the skills you test should map directly to that answer. Select questions in advance: "The best technical interview questions are open-ended, have multiple valid approaches, and reveal reasoning rather than recall." Pilot new questions internally first. Send candidates a clear brief 24–48 hours ahead covering duration, format, what to bring, and who they'll meet. During the interview, take specific notes on what candidates said and did — "Candidate immediately asked about edge cases" is useful; "seemed sharp" is not. Beyond code, assess communication, collaboration signals, problem framing, code quality, and edge-case awareness. Hold a structured debrief with scorecards submitted independently before the group call.

**Source 2: Expert Hire, "How to conduct a technical interview you can actually defend," https://www.experthire.io/blog/how-to-conduct-a-technical-interview**

Ask every candidate for the same role the same core questions, in the same order, with the same time budget: "Consistency is not bureaucracy; it is the only way to compare two candidates honestly." Level questions to seniority — juniors get mechanics questions, seniors get trade-offs and judgment. Common mistakes: trivia over reasoning, improvised questions per candidate, gut-feel scoring ("'I liked them' is where bias hides"), and talking too much ("The candidate should be doing most of the talking and reasoning").

**Source 3: daily.dev Recruiter, "Technical Interview Best Practices: Reducing Bias and Improving Signal," https://recruiter.daily.dev/resources/technical-interview-best-practices-reducing-bias-improving-signal/**

Build rubrics around 5–7 core competencies (problem decomposition, code quality, system design trade-offs, testing strategy, communication), each on a 1–5 numerical scale tied to specific, measurable behaviors — for example, "provided clear examples of resolving technical disagreements" rather than "seemed like a team player." Weight competencies by role importance and set minimum thresholds to avoid hiring candidates with critical gaps. Match format to role: live coding for real-time problem-solving, take-homes for independent work, system design for senior and staff engineers focused on architectural thinking.

**Source 4: Centum Search, "Technical Interview Process: A Hiring Manager's Guide," https://centumsearch.com/blog/technical-interview-process-hiring-managers-guide/**

After a take-home or coding assessment, hold a debrief conversation: "This is often more revealing than the code itself. It surfaces communication skills, self-awareness, and the reasoning behind their decisions." To assess communication, ask a candidate to explain a technical concept as if speaking to a non-engineer and watch whether they calibrate their language or get lost in jargon. For collaboration, ask candidates to describe a time they disagreed with a technical decision and how they handled it.

---

**Unverified**

- Statistics from approved sources (Gartner, SHRM, LinkedIn, etc.) on technical interview effectiveness or pass rates were not found in this step.
- Best practices specific to data science or non-engineering technical roles (e.g., finance, operations) were not found.

**Statistics**

1. **26%** — Structured interviews are tied with general cognitive ability tests as the second-best predictor of job performance, each with 26% predictive power, behind work sample tests at 29%. Source and publication: ERE, citing Laszlo Bock / Google re:Work. "Why Structured Interviews Are the Best Way to Hire," ERE, 2017. https://www.ere.net/why-structured-interviews-are-the-best-way-to-hire/

2. **39%** — Share of HR leaders who say structured interviews help reduce bias, per a 2020 Gartner survey. Source: Gartner, as cited by Glassdoor. Publication: Glassdoor. "11 Must-Ask Behavioral Interview Questions," Glassdoor, 2025. https://www.glassdoor.com/blog/11-must-ask-behavioral-interview-questions/

3. **78%** — Share of organizations that report pre-employment assessments used during the interview process have improved quality of hire. Source and publication: SHRM. "2024 Talent Trends Report," SHRM, 2024. https://www.shrm.org/content/dam/en/shrm/research/2024-talent-trends-research-overall-findings.pdf

4. **75%** — Share of job seekers more likely to apply to a company that actively manages its employer brand; and **78%** say the overall candidate experience signals how a company values its people. Source: Glassdoor research. Publication: Glassdoor. "A Guide to the Ultimate Candidate Experience," Glassdoor, 2026. https://www.glassdoor.com/blog/a-guide-to-the-ultimate-candidate-experience/

5. **68%** — Share of candidates who say a company's hiring process positively or negatively impacts their decision to accept a job offer. Source and publication: SHRM. "Interview Most Critical Part of Hiring Process, Candidates Say," SHRM. https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/interview-critical-part-hiring-process-candidates-say

6. **82%** — Share of recruiters who have lost a top candidate because of a poor interview experience. Source: Aptitude Research, as cited by Glassdoor. Publication: Glassdoor. "How to Improve Your Interview Process," Glassdoor, 2025. https://www.glassdoor.com/blog/improve-interview-process/

7. **41 days** — Average U.S. time to fill an open role in 2024, down from 48 days in 2023. Source and publication: SHRM. "2024 Talent Trends / Recruiter Nation benchmarking data," as cited in SHRM, 2024. https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/recruiters-express-optimism-for-2025

8. **7 of the top 10** — Companies with the highest-rated candidate experiences conduct structured interviews. Source and publication: ERE. "5 Research-Backed Ways to Improve Your Interviews," ERE. https://www.ere.net/articles/5-research-backed-ways-to-improve-your-interviews

---

**Unverified**

- Could not verify a current, URL-backed statistic from an approved source (Gartner, Gallup, SHRM, etc.) measuring the percentage of companies using structured vs. unstructured interviews in 2024–2025.
- Could not verify a statistic from an approved source on the specific predictive validity improvement rate of behavioral interviews over traditional interviews with a verifiable URL.

content.title: A Comprehensive Guide to Interviews
content.meta_description: Learn how to run a great interview process: types of interviews, question design, scoring, bias, feedback, and rejection done right.
content.main_image_alt: Hiring manager and candidate sitting across from each other during a structured job interview in a modern office setting
content.body_html:
If you find all the different types of interviews confusing, or feel like every interview is a blur, this guide will make everything about interviewing clearer. An interview is a meeting between a candidate and one or more persons in which the employer, or the employer's representatives, asks a series of questions.

Interviewing is where hiring decisions get made, and it is more varied than the word suggests. A phone screening that runs ten minutes and a final conversation with a founder that runs an hour are both interviews. So are behavioral questions that ask a candidate to describe what they did, situational questions that ask what they would do, and technical challenges that ask them to do it live. The format varies by stage and by role, and so do the scoring methods, the question types, the panel composition, and the feedback that closes the process for every candidate who does not get the offer.

This article covers every stage: the types of interviews and what each one is for, how to design questions, how to score candidates consistently, where bias enters and how to reduce it, how to run the conversation well, and how to close the loop with candidates who were not selected.

The Interview Process, Stage by Stage

Most hiring processes follow the same general arc: an initial screen, one or more interviews of increasing depth, and a final conversation before the offer. Understanding where each type of interview fits helps you design a process that moves efficiently without cutting corners. Each stage has a different purpose, and confusing them wastes time on both sides.

Phone screenings

A phone screening is a brief call — sometimes as short as ten minutes — in which the employer verifies basic qualifications, clarifies outstanding questions from the application, and confirms the candidate's continued interest. Its purpose is to create a shortlist before anyone invests time in a formal interview. A good screening call covers the candidate's current situation, their interest in the role, any hard requirements like location or compensation, and a rough sense of fit. It is not a full interview, and treating it as one wastes everyone's time.

The screening also sets the tone for the candidate's experience with your company. A well-prepared, organized screening call signals that the rest of the process will be run the same way.

Video and in-person interviews

Live interviews — whether on video or in person — make up the core of most hiring processes. A live video interview takes place online between the employer and the candidate in real time. A one-way video interview uses a platform that presents pre-recorded questions, which the candidate answers on their own time while recording their responses. In-person interviews give both parties more social information than a screen does, which matters for some roles and teams more than others. Neither format is universally superior; the right choice depends on the role, the stage, and where the team is located.

Panel interviews

A panel interview involves two or more interviewers — who may include HR representatives, hiring managers, and team leads — sitting together to question a single candidate. It gives multiple stakeholders ownership of the hiring decision and can eliminate the need for several separate rounds. In a group interview, panel members take turns asking questions, with some present only to observe. Panels are efficient, but they require coordination: everyone on the panel should review the candidate's materials and know which questions they are responsible for before the interview begins. For the debrief, have the most junior interviewer speak first so honest disagreement gets voiced before senior opinions set the tone.

Final interviews

A final interview is typically the last conversation before a decision is made. It often involves a more senior person than earlier rounds — a founder, a department head, or an executive — and tends to focus less on technical qualifications and more on alignment, values, and long-term fit. By this stage, the question is rarely whether the candidate can do the job. It is whether both sides want to move forward together.

Interview Types and What Each One Tests

Beyond the stage of the process, the format of each interview determines what information you can gather. Here are the main types, and what each one is built to reveal.

Behavioral interviews

Behavioral interviews focus on actions candidates have taken in previous jobs. The principle is that past performance can predict future behavior. Questions typically begin with "Tell me about a time when…" or "Give me an example of a time when…." The interviewer assesses how the candidate approached and resolved real work problems, rather than what they claim they would do in a hypothetical. Behavioral questions are among the most reliable question types because the candidate has to draw on actual experience, which is harder to fabricate than a speculative answer.

The STAR method — Situation, Task, Action, Result — gives candidates a structure for answering behavioral questions and gives interviewers a consistent framework for evaluating the answers. When answers are vague or rehearsed, follow-up probes like "What specifically did you do in that situation?" or "What would you handle differently now?" tend to surface more useful information.

Situational interviews

Situational questions present a hypothetical scenario and ask the candidate how they would respond. Starters include "What would you do if…" and "Tell me how you would handle…." They test a candidate's ability to reason through problems and think on their feet, but they reveal less about actual work history than behavioral questions do. A candidate who has never encountered the scenario before can still give a thoughtful answer — which is both the value and the limitation of this format. Situational questions work best alongside behavioral ones, not in place of them.

Technical interviews

Technical interviews ask candidates to solve problems live, complete coding challenges, or walk through case analyses using the tools and frameworks specific to the job. They are common for engineering, data, and finance roles and are typically the longest individual interview format, running one to three hours. The best technical interview questions are open-ended, have multiple valid approaches, and reveal reasoning rather than recall. A candidate who asks good questions, explains their thinking clearly, and considers edge cases shows more than a candidate who arrives at the right answer in silence.

Consistency matters in technical interviews as much as anywhere else. Asking every candidate for the same role the same core questions, in the same order, with the same time budget, is the only way to compare two candidates honestly. Scoring on gut feel — "I liked them" — is exactly where bias enters the picture.

Case interviews

In a case interview, each applicant receives a hypothetical or existing business problem to analyze, draws on knowledge and creative thinking to propose a solution, and explains how they arrived at it. Case interviews are common in consulting and strategy roles. What they reveal is not whether the candidate reaches the right answer — often there is no single right answer — but how they frame the problem, what questions they ask, and how they communicate their reasoning under pressure.

Structured vs. Unstructured Interviewing

How you run an interview matters as much as which questions you ask. The difference between structured and unstructured interviewing is one of the most consequential distinctions in hiring.

A structured interview standardizes the questions and evaluation methods used: each candidate for the same role receives the same questions in the same order and is scored against the same criteria. An unstructured interview involves a relatively unplanned conversation that differs across candidates, aiming to get a "feel for" the person rather than evaluating against a fixed set of criteria. Structured interviews are tied with general cognitive ability tests as the second-best predictor of job performance, each with 26% predictive power, behind work sample tests at 29%, according to ERE's analysis of research by Laszlo Bock. An unstructured conversation gives the interviewer a strong impression, but impressions are not the same as evidence.

The case for structure goes beyond accuracy. According to Gartner, as reported by Glassdoor, 39% of HR leaders say structured interviews help reduce bias. ERE also reports that seven of the top ten companies with the highest-rated candidate experiences conduct structured interviews — which suggests that consistency and rigor are not at odds with a positive candidate experience. They tend to reinforce each other.

Designing Questions That Produce Useful Answers

The questions you ask determine the information available when you make your decision. Generic questions produce generic answers. Questions rooted in the actual work of the role produce answers you can evaluate against something real.

Start by defining the competencies the role requires. For each competency, write questions that ask the candidate to demonstrate it, not just claim it. "Tell me about a time when you had to deliver difficult news to a client" is a stronger question than "Are you comfortable with difficult conversations?" because the candidate has to show, not assert. For unique interview questions organized by competency and paired with scoring rubrics, the linked article covers both the questions and how to evaluate the answers consistently. For problem-solving interview questions specifically, there are ten examples with guidance on what strong answers look like and what constitutes a red flag.

Avoid questions that touch on protected characteristics — arrest record, military status, pregnancy, age, religion, marital status, and others. These questions create legal risk and have no place in a fair hiring process. Forbes notes that managers should never leave a candidate wondering whether small talk about their place of worship or sexual orientation may have cost them the job. Sticking to job-relevant questions protects both the candidate and the company, and makes your process easier to defend.

Scoring Candidates Consistently

A question only does its job if the answer is evaluated against something fixed. Without a scoring framework, two interviewers watching the same candidate give the same answer can reach opposite conclusions — and neither of them is wrong by their own reasoning. That is the problem a scorecard solves.

An interview scorecard lists predetermined criteria used to evaluate candidates. Interviewers score each candidate against the criteria immediately after the interview, while the conversation is fresh. A useful scorecard includes the competencies the role requires, a rating scale, space for specific examples and direct quotes, and an overall recommendation field. As The Predictive Index puts it: scoring criteria defined after a strong candidate impresses you are not criteria anymore — they are rationalizations.

Behaviorally anchored rating scales (BARS) go further by spelling out what each score looks like in observable behavior. That gives two interviewers a much better shot at rating the same answer the same way. For a full template and step-by-step instructions, the article on the behavioral interview scoring matrix covers how to build one, how to use it, and what a completed matrix looks like.

SHRM's 2024 Talent Trends Report found that 78% of organizations report pre-employment assessments used during the interview process have improved quality of hire. A scorecard is the most direct way to bring that discipline into every interview your team conducts.

Interview Bias and Where It Enters the Process

Interview bias is any preference or mental shortcut that shapes how an interviewer judges a candidate on factors unrelated to their ability to do the job. Most of these judgments happen quickly and feel like sound instinct to the person making them, which is what makes them so difficult to catch from the inside.

Common types include first impression bias, the halo and horns effect, affinity bias, confirmation bias, the contrast effect, recency and primacy bias, stereotype bias, and groupthink. Each enters the process at a different point. First impression bias forms before the candidate has answered a single question. Confirmation bias shapes how the interviewer hears the answers once an early impression is set. The contrast effect distorts scores when a weaker candidate precedes a strong one, or vice versa. Groupthink suppresses honest disagreement when the most senior person in the room speaks first.

Structure is the most reliable tool against bias, but not the only one. Using diverse panels, standardizing questions, and having the most junior interviewer speak first in a debrief all help. For a full account of each bias type and practical fixes for small and larger hiring teams alike, the article on interview bias covers all eight types in depth. For a closer look at how the first few seconds of a conversation shape everything that follows, the article on first impression bias examines that dynamic and gives specific tactics to counter it.

Running the Interview Well

Good interview design only works if the conversation itself is run well. Several practices consistently improve what you learn and how the candidate experiences the process.

Prepare before the conversation

Brief the panel in advance. Everyone should review the resume, the job description, and any screening notes before the interview, not during it. Assign specific questions to each panel member so the conversation covers what it needs to and nothing important is repeated or skipped. Consider sending interview questions to candidates at least 24 hours in advance — research from the University of Wisconsin suggests this reduces nerves and produces more thoughtful answers without compromising the information you get.

Let the candidate talk

Aim for the candidate to carry roughly 80% of the conversation. Resist the urge to fill silence, elaborate on the question, or jump in before the candidate has finished thinking. The purpose of the interview is to learn about the candidate, and that requires the candidate to do the talking. Reserve at least ten minutes at the end for the candidate's questions — their questions often reveal as much about their thinking as their answers do.

Take specific notes

Notes taken during or immediately after an interview are more reliable than memory. "Candidate immediately asked about edge cases" is a useful note. "Seemed sharp" is not. Specific observations — what the candidate said, how they approached a problem, what they asked — give you something to return to when you debrief. They also give you a record if a hiring decision is ever questioned.

Share an itinerary with the candidate

Candidates who know what to expect perform closer to their actual ability. Sharing an interview itinerary — the format, the duration, who they'll meet, and what to prepare — costs nothing and signals that your company runs an organized process. Forbes notes that finishing the full interview with every candidate regardless of early impressions also matters: cutting an interview short based on disinterest invites reputational risk and denies the candidate a fair chance. According to SHRM, 68% of candidates say a company's hiring process positively or negatively affects their decision to accept a job offer. The interview is the most visible part of that process.

Keeping Your Hiring Legally Sound

The interview process carries legal obligations that go beyond common sense. Questions about protected characteristics — including age, religion, marital status, pregnancy, national origin, disability, and others — are off-limits regardless of how casually they come up in conversation. This applies to formal questions and to small talk. A hiring manager who asks where a candidate's name is from, or whether they plan to have children, may not intend harm, but the legal exposure is real and the candidate's experience suffers for it.

The discipline of using consistent, job-relevant questions for every candidate protects both sides. It keeps the conversation on the work — which is where it belongs — and makes your decisions defensible if they are ever challenged. This is another reason structured interviews matter: they make it easier to hold the line on what gets asked, and to show, if needed, that every candidate was treated the same way. For a view of how the interview fits into the full sequence of hiring decisions, the article on hiring process steps covers the whole arc from job post to offer.

Giving Feedback After the Interview

Interview feedback is the final stage of the hiring process, closing it in a respectful manner. It is usually given to candidates who were not selected, explaining why and offering actionable guidance for improvement. Most companies skip it. The ones that give it well build a reputation that draws better candidates over time.

Generic feedback — "we went with someone who was a stronger fit" — does nothing for the candidate and signals that the employer did not engage seriously with their application. Specific, actionable feedback, delivered promptly, is a different matter. It treats the candidate as someone who invested real time and preparation in the process. Glassdoor research finds that 78% of job seekers say the overall candidate experience signals how a company values its people, and feedback is a direct expression of that. The article on interview feedback examples gives word-for-word scripts for eight rejection scenarios — from a skills gap to a cultural misalignment — along with guidance on how to standardize and automate the process.

Handling Rejection with Care

Rejection is part of every hiring process. How you handle it shapes how candidates think about your company long after the process ends. A candidate who receives a prompt, respectful rejection email is far more likely to refer others to your company, apply again in the future, or speak well of their experience. A candidate who hears nothing — or hears back weeks later with a form letter — remembers that too.

Aptitude Research, as cited by Glassdoor, found that 82% of recruiters have lost a top candidate because of a poor interview experience. Rejection is part of that experience. Sending the message promptly, using the candidate's name, referencing the role they applied for, and keeping the tone respectful are the basics. For templates covering every stage of the hiring process, the article on candidate rejection email templates gives language you can use and adapt. The article on writing personalized job rejection emails explains how to make each one feel like it came from a person who paid attention.

Trade-offs Worth Knowing Before You Design Your Process

Structure improves consistency and reduces bias, but it comes with real trade-offs. A tightly scripted interview can feel mechanical to both sides, and some of the most useful signal in a conversation comes from an unexpected exchange — a question the candidate asks, a direction the conversation takes naturally. The goal is not to eliminate flexibility but to ensure that every candidate is evaluated against the same criteria, whatever path the conversation takes to get there.

Behavioral interviews rely on past experience, which means candidates who are early in their careers or changing fields may have fewer direct examples to draw on. Situational questions can fill that gap, though they test reasoning rather than track record. Technical interviews are reliable for assessing hard skills but can disadvantage candidates who perform better in context than under artificial time pressure. Case interviews reveal how someone thinks but can be practiced extensively in advance, which reduces what they signal about native ability. No single interview format tells the whole story, which is why the most reliable processes combine several.

Build a Process Where Every Interview Counts

A well-designed interview process gives you a consistent, defensible basis for every hiring decision. It treats candidates fairly, produces comparable data across the applicant pool, and reduces the chance that a strong candidate is dismissed for the wrong reason or a weak one advances on a good impression. The investment in structure — writing the questions before you meet anyone, building the scorecard before the first candidate arrives, briefing the panel and assigning roles — returns better decisions and a stronger reputation over time.

faq_items.q: What is the difference between a structured and an unstructured interview?
faq_items.a: A structured interview gives every candidate the same questions in the same order and evaluates each answer against the same predetermined criteria. An unstructured interview follows no fixed script and varies by candidate, aiming to get a general sense of fit. Structured interviews are more reliable predictors of job performance and make it easier to compare candidates fairly.

faq_items.q: What is a behavioral interview question?
faq_items.a: A behavioral interview question asks a candidate to describe a specific situation they handled in a previous role, drawing on the principle that past behavior predicts future performance. These questions typically begin with "Tell me about a time when…" or "Give me an example of a time you…." They produce more reliable answers than hypothetical questions because the candidate must draw on real experience.

faq_items.q: How many interview rounds should a hiring process have?
faq_items.a: Most hiring processes include a phone screening, one or two structured interviews, and a final conversation before the offer. The right number depends on the seniority of the role, the number of stakeholders, and what information still needs to be gathered at each stage. Adding rounds beyond what the decision requires slows the process and risks losing candidates to faster-moving employers.

faq_items.q: How should you score candidates after an interview?
faq_items.a: Score candidates immediately after each interview using a scorecard that lists the competencies the role requires, a consistent rating scale, and space for specific observations and direct quotes. Scoring before the debrief conversation prevents one strong impression from overriding the evidence. Behaviorally anchored rating scales, which describe what each score looks like in observable behavior, make scores more consistent across interviewers.

faq_items.q: What is interview bias, and how do you reduce it?
faq_items.a: Interview bias is any preference or mental shortcut that shapes how an interviewer judges a candidate on factors unrelated to the job. Common types include first impression bias, the halo and horns effect, affinity bias, and confirmation bias. Structured interviews, diverse panels, standardized scoring, and having the most junior interviewer speak first in a debrief all reduce its influence.

faq_items.q: Should you give candidates feedback after an interview?
faq_items.a: Yes, particularly for candidates who reached an interview stage. Specific, actionable feedback delivered promptly treats candidates with respect, reinforces your employer brand, and encourages strong candidates to apply again or refer others. Generic feedback — "we went with a stronger fit" — provides no value and signals that the employer did not engage seriously with the candidate's application.

faq_items.q: What questions are off-limits in a job interview?
faq_items.a: Questions about protected characteristics — including age, religion, marital status, pregnancy, national origin, disability, and military status — are off-limits in a job interview, whether asked formally or as small talk. Only questions directly related to the candidate's ability to perform the job are appropriate. Using a consistent, pre-written question set for every candidate is the most reliable way to keep the conversation on the right ground.
